title: Compact derivative estimate for smooth matrix-weighted composition
statement:
Over $\mathbf R$ [def-weil-field], let $d,m,q,r\geq0$, let $O\subseteq\mathbf R^d$ and $P\subseteq\mathbf R^m$ be open, and let $g:O\to P$ and $A:O\to\operatorname{Mat}_{r\times q}(\mathbf R)$ be smooth (each coordinate has continuous derivatives of every finite order). For any smooth $f:P\to\mathbf R^q$, put $T_{A,g}f(z)=A(z)f(g(z))$. This function is smooth on $O$. Given a compact $S\subseteq O$ and an integer $k\geq0$, there is a constant $C>0$, depending on $A,g,S,k$ but not on $f$, such that
$$\max_{|\alpha|\leq k}\sup_{z\in S}\|\partial^\alpha(T_{A,g}f)(z)\|\leq C\max_{|\beta|\leq k}\sup_{w\in g(S)}\|\partial^\beta f(w)\|.$$
Here a multi-index is a tuple of nonnegative integers, its order is the sum of its entries, $\partial^\alpha$ is the corresponding repeated coordinate derivative, and the norms are Euclidean. Supremum over the empty compact set and the norm in a zero-dimensional target are $0$.

source.place: WANTED locally: Part I §3.A–3.B, inherited pp.11–13 not independently verified. Agent-stated Euclidean auxiliary estimate for the test-density topology; no claim that the unavailable document states this formula.

proof.text: Write $H=T_{A,g}f$. Its $a$-th scalar component is $H_a=\sum_{b=1}^q A_{ab}(f_b\circ g)$. The cited smooth sum, product and composition rules show that every $H_a$ is smooth, hence $H$ is smooth by the coordinate definition. This also covers an empty sum or zero-dimensional target. For any smooth scalar $h$, $\partial_i h(z)=Dh(z)[e_i]$ is smooth: the differential is smooth and evaluation on a fixed basis vector is a continuous linear map. Repetition gives smoothness of every coordinate derivative of $A,g,f$ and $H$. All these are local assertions on the given open domains; no extension across their boundaries is asserted.

source.place: Agent application of smooth calculus; ContDiff/Comp.lean:223,724; ContDiff/Operations.lean:184,450, and the corresponding clauses of lem-sfb-real-smooth-differentiation.

proof.text: Applied to a smooth scalar $h$ and coordinate vectors, second-differential symmetry gives $\partial_i\partial_j h=\partial_j\partial_i h$. Indeed evaluation on a fixed vector is linear, so differentiating $Dh[e_j]$ gives $D(Dh)[e_i][e_j]$. Apply this to every smooth derivative of $h$ from step 1. Swapping adjacent coordinate derivatives therefore sorts any finite derivative word without changing its value. Thus, for the multi-index convention in the statement, $\partial_i(\partial^\beta h)=\partial^{\beta+e_i}h$. The assertion is vacuous when there are no coordinate directions.

source.place: Agent adjacent-swap argument from ContDiffAt.isSymmSndFDerivAt:533–534 and IsSymmSndFDerivAt.eq:98–101; smooth derivatives from step 1.

proof.text:
Induct on $|\alpha|$, simultaneously for every $a,b$, to construct smooth scalar coefficients $c_{\alpha\beta ab}$ on $O$, independent of $f$, such that
$$\partial^\alpha H_a=\sum_{b=1}^q\sum_{|\beta|\leq|\alpha|}c_{\alpha\beta ab}(\partial^\beta f_b)\circ g.$$
At order zero set $c_{0,0,ab}=A_{ab}$. For each nonzero $\alpha$, choose once and for all $i$ with $\alpha_i>0$ and put $\gamma=\alpha-e_i$. Differentiate the already constructed formula for $\gamma$. The product and chain rules, evaluated on $e_i$, replace a term $c(\partial^\beta f_b)\circ g$ by
$$(\partial_i c)(\partial^\beta f_b)\circ g+\sum_{j=1}^m c\,\partial_i g_j\,(\partial^{\beta+e_j}f_b)\circ g.$$
Here the chain formula follows by expanding $Dg[e_i]=\sum_j(\partial_i g_j)e_j$ and using linearity of the outer differential; step 2 sorts its derivatives. Collect equal indices, explicitly setting
$$c_{\alpha\beta ab}=\partial_i c_{\gamma\beta ab}+\sum_{j:\beta_j>0}c_{\gamma,\beta-e_j,ab}\,\partial_i g_j,$$
where coefficients outside $|\beta|\leq|\gamma|$ are zero. This proves the inductive identity and smoothness using step 1. Every coefficient depends only on $A,g,\alpha,\beta,a,b$. If $d=0$, only $\alpha=0$ occurs; if $m=0$, the chain sum is empty.

source.place: Agent induction from HasFDerivAt.comp:105–107 and FDeriv/Mul.lean HasFDerivAt.mul:205–209; no higher chain-rule formula is assumed.

proof.text: If $S=\varnothing$, take $C=1$ and the estimate is $0\leq0$. Assume henceforth $S\ne\varnothing$. Put $B=\{\beta\in\mathbf N^m:|\beta|\leq k\}$ and $N=|B|\geq1$; it is finite since each entry lies between $0$ and $k$. There are also finitely many $\alpha\in\mathbf N^d$ with $|\alpha|\leq k$. For each coefficient in step 3 at these orders, extend it by zero outside $O$. This extension is continuous on $S$: near each point of $S\subset O$ it equals the smooth coefficient. Apply the cited compact norm bound (with scalar target identified with $\mathbf R^1$). Taking the maximum of $1$ and the finitely many resulting real bounds gives $M\geq1$ with $|c_{\alpha\beta ab}(z)|\leq M$ on $S$. Extend missing coefficients by zero. Crucially $M$ is chosen solely from $A,g,S,k$, before choosing $f$. If $q=0$ or $r=0$ there are no such coefficients and take $M=1$.

source.place: Agent finite-maximum argument using IsCompact.exists_bound_of_continuousOn, additive declaration generated at lines 96–100.

proof.text:
For each $\beta\in B$, the map $z\mapsto(\partial^\beta f)(g(z))$ is smooth on $O$ by step 1. Its zero extension is continuous on $S$ for the same local reason as in step 4. The compact norm bound therefore bounds its norm on $S$, equivalently the norm of $\partial^\beta f$ on $g(S)$. Thus
$$P_f=\max_{\beta\in B}\sup_{w\in g(S)}\|\partial^\beta f(w)\|$$
is finite and nonnegative. The image $g(S)$ is indeed compact: pull any open cover back along continuous $g$, use a finite subcover of $S$, and then map it forward. No openness or unique-differentiability property of $g(S)$ is needed. Every scalar component satisfies $|\partial^\beta f_b(g(z))|\leq\|\partial^\beta f(g(z))\|\leq P_f$ by the Euclidean norm formula and the supremum definition.

source.place: Agent application of IsCompact.exists_bound_of_continuousOn:96–100 to derivative compositions; smoothness supplied by lem-sfb-real-smooth-differentiation.

proof.text: The expansion and scalar triangle inequality give $|\partial^\alpha H_a(z)|\leq qNMP_f$ for every $|\alpha|\leq k$ and $z\in S$. For $v\in\mathbf R^r$, writing $v=\sum_a v_a e_a$ and using $\|e_a\|=1$ gives $\|v\|\leq\sum_a|v_a|$. Hence $\|\partial^\alpha H(z)\|\leq rqNMP_f$. Take $C=1+rqNM>0$, independent of $f$, and then take the supremum over $S$ and the finite maximum over $\alpha$. This is exactly the claimed inequality. For $q=0$ or $r=0$, $H$ is zero and this formula gives $C=1$; for $m=0$, $B=\{0\}$ and $N=1$. The order-zero case uses the same expansion without differentiation.

source.place: Agent finite-sum Euclidean norm calculation from the identities and bounds in steps 3–5.
